cards.title: Unconditional zero knowledge for gap circuit complexity
cards.formal: Is there a fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) for which \(\mathrm{Gap}_{\varepsilon}\mathrm{MCSP}\) admits a computational zero-knowledge interactive proof system without a computational hardness assumption? Given the length-\(N=2^n\) truth table of a Boolean function, the promise distinguishes circuit size at most \(N^\varepsilon\) from size greater than \(N^{1-\varepsilon}\). This card selects the MCSP branch of the original question and the gap family used by Hirahara and Nanashima; it does not claim equivalence with every MINKT or other gap variant.

source_formulation.text: Does (some gap version of) MCSP or MINKT admit a computational zero knowledge proof system?

cards.why: Would provide a natural unconditional zero-knowledge protocol for a central problem about circuit descriptions. It probes the connection between worst-case complexity, average-case cryptographic hardness and verification that reveals no efficiently usable information beyond the claim.

upgraded_from.title: Zero knowledge for gap meta-complexity problems

cards.definitions:
The common input is the full truth table \(x\) of a function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), with \(n\geq1\) and \(N=2^n\). Let \(C(f)\) be its minimum Boolean circuit size. Fix the standard basis of binary AND and OR and unary NOT, with constant inputs available, arbitrary fan-out, one output, and size equal to the number of gates. Circuits are acyclic and compute every truth-table entry correctly.

A yes-instance satisfies \(C(f)\leq N^\varepsilon\). A no-instance satisfies \(C(f)>N^{1-\varepsilon}\). Inputs between these thresholds have no required decision outcome. The strict no-threshold follows the formal definition in the later source; the thresholds need not be integers. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, not supplied per instance. The task has both low-complexity and high-complexity promised inputs at arbitrarily large lengths.

An interactive proof has an honest prover \(P\) and a randomized verifier \(V\). Total communication, rounds and verifier computation are polynomial in \(N\), the explicit truth-table length. No computational bound is imposed on the prover. On every yes-instance, the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(2/3\). On every no-instance, every cheating prover, including an unbounded one, causes acceptance with probability at most \(1/3\). This is a proof system; soundness only against efficient provers would be an argument system.

Computational zero knowledge requires that for every randomized polynomial-time verifier \(V^*\), including one given arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information \(z\), there is a randomized polynomial-time simulator \(S_{V^*}\). Given only \(x,z\), it produces a distribution computationally indistinguishable from the entire view of \(V^*\) in the honest-prover interaction on \(x\). That view includes the common input, auxiliary information, verifier randomness, messages and final output. The simulator is not given a small circuit or other witness.

Indistinguishability is required on all yes-instances: every polynomial-size distinguishing circuit has only negligible advantage in \(N\), uniformly over these instances and polynomial-length auxiliary strings. Negligible means smaller than \(N^{-c}\) for every fixed positive \(c\) at sufficiently large \(N\). The simulator and verifier use the ordinary polynomial-time convention of the later source. No setup, random oracle, trusted third party or hardness assumption is supplied.

The chosen circuit basis fixes a concrete representation. The existential constant-gap formulation tolerates constant-factor changes of standard finite bases by choosing a slightly wider gap and handling finitely many small lengths separately. It does not identify circuits with a shortest program: MINKT instead bounds the program length needed to print a string within a supplied time budget, and its gap parameters constitute a separate choice.

The target asks for one protocol meeting worst-case completeness, soundness and zero knowledge at every input length. A protocol that succeeds on most inputs from a particular distribution or only at infinitely many lengths is a weaker result.
cards.answer_criterion: Give some fixed admissible gap constant and a protocol with proofs of polynomial verifier and simulator cost, completeness, soundness against all provers, and computational zero knowledge against arbitrary efficient auxiliary-input verifiers, without assuming one-way functions or another hardness premise. A negative answer must rule out the specified protocols for every constant in this selected gap family. Failure for that family would not by itself refute all alternatives in the original broader question.

context_blocks.title: A small circuit is easy to verify but may reveal information
context_blocks.text: Yes-instances have polynomially checkable small-circuit witnesses, so this is a promise problem in NP. Revealing the entire witness supplies an ordinary proof, but does not establish zero knowledge.

context_blocks.title: Hardness assumptions already give protocols
context_blocks.text: The standard one-way-function theorem supplies zero-knowledge proofs for NP. The original question asks for an unconditional result; the case where the problem is worst-case hard but suitable cryptographic hardness is unavailable is not covered by that theorem.

context_blocks.title: Unconditional average-case progress has weaker quantifiers
context_blocks.text: Ilango, Ren and Santhanam obtain infinitely-often average-case protocols, with locally samplable distributions in their MCSP statement. That does not give a protocol correct on every promised input at every length.

context_blocks.title: The later equivalence retains a separate hardness premise
context_blocks.text: Hirahara and Nanashima characterize one-way functions using both membership of the gap problem in CZK and worst-case hardness of CZK. The theorem does not establish the gap problem’s unconditional CZK membership. Their 2024 full version also distinguishes errorless average-case schemes from error-prone ones.

cards.context:
Yes-instances have polynomially checkable small-circuit witnesses, so this is a promise problem in NP. Revealing the entire witness supplies an ordinary proof, but does not establish zero knowledge.

The standard one-way-function theorem supplies zero-knowledge proofs for NP. The original question asks for an unconditional result; the case where the problem is worst-case hard but suitable cryptographic hardness is unavailable is not covered by that theorem.

Ilango, Ren and Santhanam obtain infinitely-often average-case protocols, with locally samplable distributions in their MCSP statement. That does not give a protocol correct on every promised input at every length.

Hirahara and Nanashima characterize one-way functions using both membership of the gap problem in CZK and worst-case hardness of CZK. The theorem does not establish the gap problem’s unconditional CZK membership. Their 2024 full version also distinguishes errorless average-case schemes from error-prone ones.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
